tasks.heading: Task 1 — Culinary terms and common trade names
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — culinary terms and common trade names for ingredients used to produce chocolate confectionery, and for the individual chocolates prepared.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: Name plus 20–35 words in each writing cell.
tasks.scenario: You are a new commis chocolatier at La Meridienne Patisserie, Rundle Street, Adelaide. The head chocolatier uses trade terms on the production board and expects you to use them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what each ingredient is and how you use it in chocolate work. Give an accepted culinary or trade synonym. You may add an Australian brand example, but it is not required. Complete the table.

headers: What it is and how it is used in chocolate work

parts.modelAnswer:
Couverture | Pure coating chocolate, cocoa butter at least 31%~~Fluid enough to cast thin shells, enrobe and dip~~Must be tempered before use | Coating chocolate or pure chocolate~~Sold as callets, pistoles or buttons
Cocoa butter | Natural fat pressed from the cocoa bean~~Carries flavour and sets hard on cooling~~Crystallises during tempering~~Added in small amounts to thin couverture | Cacao butter~~Tinted form sold as coloured cocoa butter
Praliné | Paste of caramelised nuts, usually almonds or hazelnuts~~Ground smooth or left textured~~Used as a filling in its own right~~Folded through ganache or blended with couverture | Praline paste or nut praline~~French pralines, not Belgian praline
Gianduja | Soft blend of couverture, ground roasted hazelnuts and sugar~~Softens at body temperature~~Piped as a centre, or cut and dipped rather than moulded thin | Gianduia~~Hazelnut chocolate paste
Fondant | Cooked sugar syrup boiled to about 116-121 degrees C~~Agitated so it crystallises to a white opaque paste~~Warmed and flavoured for soft, sweet bonbon centres | Sugar fondant~~Poured fondant
Invert sugar | Syrup of sucrose split into glucose and fructose~~Holds moisture and softens texture~~Slows crystallisation~~Keeps ganache and fondant centres smooth for longer | Trimoline or invert syrup~~Glucose syrup and honey give the same effect

All sixteen (b) cells complete, with the correct culinary or trade name for each of the eight descriptions.

Fourteen of sixteen (b) cells correct.

Praline in (a) confused with the Belgian moulded praline.
Fewer than six of the eight (b) descriptions matched to an Appendix A product.
A product named that does not appear in Appendix A.
Answers copied word for word from the learner resource.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Defined all six terms accurately with correct trade names, and matched all eight descriptions to the right Appendix A products, listing A3, A4 and A5 for the moulded shell. Meets the Knowledge Evidence for culinary terms and trade names - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: Terms were defined loosely and praline described as a filled Belgian shell, not a nut paste. Three (b) descriptions matched no Appendix A product. tasks.heading: Task 2 — Date codes, rotation labels and ingredient quality
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — contents of date codes and rotation labels for stock (primary); indicators of freshness and quality of stocked ingredients for chocolates.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: (a) 120 words · (b) 25–35 words per cell · (c) 100 words.
tasks.scenario:
It is Monday morning at La Meridienne Patisserie, Rundle Street, Adelaide. A delivery has arrived for the week's chocolate production: dark couverture callets, fresh cream, hazelnut kernels, glacé orange and unsalted butter.
You check the delivery in and put it away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what information a date code and a stock rotation label carry. Explain how you use both when receiving this delivery and issuing stock to production.
parts.modelAnswer:
Date code is the manufacturer's shelf-life marking: a use-by or a best-before date.
Use-by: unsafe after that date. Best-before: quality falls but food may still be safe.
Printed with a batch or lot number, so product traces back to its production run.
Rotation label is applied by the kitchen, not the manufacturer.
Records product name, date received or opened, use-by date, and the labeller's initials.
On receipt: check every date code before signing; reject short-dated or out-of-date stock.
Label each item, put newest stock behind oldest, and record couverture batch numbers.

satisfactory: (a) date code carries a use-by or best-before date plus a batch or lot number.
(a) rotation label carries product, date received or opened, use-by date and labeller's initials.
(a) explains use of both on receipt and in storage, including first-in-first-out.
(b) all ten cells give genuine sensory or physical indicators for the ingredient named.
(b) every cell gives a defensible action on failure.
(c) links date coding and rotation to the food safety program.
(c) names the Food Act 2001 (SA), Standard 3.2.2, and SA Health or the council environmental health officer.
minimumAcceptable: (a) distinguishes use-by from best-before.
(a) names at least three fields on a rotation label.
(b) eight of ten cells correct.
(b) at least one indicator and one action for each of cream and nuts.
(c) names the Food Act 2001 (SA) and the regulator, with one clear link to food safety.
criticalErrors: Use-by and best-before treated as the same thing.
Cream or butter accepted without a temperature check.
A failed high-risk ingredient used anyway, downgraded or sorted.
No SA legislation, or a non-SA regulator, named in (c).
Stock rotation described as newest first.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Correctly separated use-by from best-before, listed the rotation label fields, and gave sound indicators and rejection actions for all five ingredients, including the 5 degrees C check on cream and butter. Named the Food Act 2001 (SA), Standard 3.2.2 and SA Health - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: Part (b) accepted cream on appearance alone with no temperature check, and part (c) named no legislation or regulator. Re-attempt: state the receipt temperature required for dairy and what you do if it fails, and name the SA Act, Standard and regulator - NS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each ingredient, state the freshness and quality indicators you check. State what you do if an ingredient fails the check. Complete the table.

headers: Indicators of freshness and quality you check
What you do if it fails the check

parts.modelAnswer:
Dark couverture callets | Bag sealed and undamaged, within date and batch recorded~~Callets loose and free-flowing, not clumped~~Even dark colour, no grey or white bloom~~Clean cocoa aroma, no rancid or musty smell | Reject at the door and record on the goods-inward record~~If already accepted, quarantine and label Do not use~~Report to the head chocolatier for supplier credit
Fresh cream | Delivered at 5 degrees C or below~~Use-by date not passed, carton and seal intact~~Pours freely, no thickening, lumps or separation~~Clean sweet dairy smell, no sour note | Reject the delivery~~Discard and record the reason if a temperature breach is found later~~Never use in ganache; cream is the highest-risk ingredient
Hazelnut kernels | Kernels whole and dry, no shrivelling, pale even colour~~Snap when broken~~Fresh nutty smell, no paint-like or rancid odour~~No insect damage, webbing or mould, and within date | Reject or quarantine and label it~~Rancid nuts cannot be corrected by roasting~~Fault would carry into the croquant and rocher
Glacé orange | Pieces glossy, plump and pliable, even colour~~Not hard, dried out or sugar-crusted~~Clean citrus aroma, no mould, fermentation smell or syrup leakage~~Packaging sealed and within date | Reject or quarantine and report it~~Mould or fermentation means the sugar concentration has failed~~Discard the whole pack rather than sorting it
Unsalted butter | Delivered at 5 degrees C or below, wrapper intact~~Even pale colour, no darkened or translucent edges~~Firm and cool to the touch~~Clean sweet creamy smell, no cheesy or rancid note | Reject on temperature or smell~~Butter picks up odours easily~~Discard tainted butter rather than using it~~Report the fault to the supplier

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how date coding and stock rotation support the patisserie's food safety program. Identify your obligations under the Food Act 2001 (SA) and Standard 3.2.2 of the Food Standards Code.
parts.modelAnswer:
Date coding and rotation are the practical controls that keep the food safety program working.
High-risk ingredients such as cream and butter are used within their validated shelf life.
Oldest stock moves first, so nothing is held past its date.
Every batch traces back to a supplier if a problem is found.
Requirements come from the Food Act 2001 (SA) and the Food Standards Code.
Standard 3.2.2 Food Safety Practices and General Requirements applies.
Requires all practicable measures to use only safe and suitable food, and receipt records kept.
Regulator is SA Health; day-to-day inspection by the local council's environmental health officers.

tasks.heading: Task 3 — Processes for producing different types of chocolates
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — processes for producing different types of chocolates: cut or dressed; hand coated; enrobing; made with prepared hollow shells; moulded.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: 40–55 words for the method column; product code and short reason only in the last column.
tasks.stem: Explain how you carry out each process below to produce individual chocolates. Name one Appendix A product made by that process. Give a short reason why the process suits it. Complete the table.

headers: How the process is carried out
Appendix A product and why the process suits it

parts.modelAnswer:
Cut or dressed | Firm centre such as ganache, croquant or nougat set in a frame~~Cut to uniform size with a guitar or knife~~Hand dipped in tempered couverture~~Marked before it sets | A7 almond croquant~~Croquant sets hard enough to slab and cut~~Cutting gives uniform pieces~~Dipped coat seals the sugar against moisture
Hand coated | Centres rolled or shaped by hand~~Small quantity of tempered couverture worked over by gloved hand~~Coat follows the shape rather than pooling | A2 chocolate heaven bliss ball~~Soft marzipan ball would deform in an enrober~~Gives the deliberately rough, hand-rolled look
Enrobing | Cut centres placed on the enrober belt~~Passed under a curtain of tempered couverture~~Blower and vibrating table level the coat~~Cooling tunnel sets the coat | A9 raspberry jelly square~~Squares uniform and flat, so the belt coats them evenly~~Faster by machine for the Friday order volume
Made with prepared hollow shells | Ready-made hollow shells warmed slightly~~Filled through the opening with a liquid or soft filling~~Allowed to crust~~Sealed with tempered couverture and finished | A10 orange liqueur hollow sphere~~Liquid liqueur syrup would leak from a shell cast in-house~~Pre-formed shell holds the filling
Moulded | Polished moulds filled with tempered couverture~~Vibrated and inverted to leave a thin shell~~Chilled, filled and allowed to crust~~Capped with tempered couverture and demoulded | A3 caramel bonbon~~High gloss and sharp cast shape the boxed range needs~~Sealed shell contains the soft caramel

satisfactory: All five processes explained as they are actually carried out.
Distinguishing step named: cutting a set slab; hand working the coat; the belt and curtain.
Distinguishing step named: filling and sealing a ready-made shell; casting, inverting and capping.
Each process matched to an Appendix A product that Appendix A shows using it.
Each match carries a reason drawn from the centre or the volume.

Enrobing and moulded are both right.
Each match carries a reason, not a bare product code.
criticalErrors: Enrobing described as hand dipping.
Moulding described without inverting or draining the mould.
A product matched to a process Appendix A does not show for it.
A product named that is not in Appendix A.
A match given with no reason.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Explained all five processes with the distinguishing steps and matched each to the correct Appendix A product with a sound reason, for example A9 to enrobing on uniform flat squares and run volume. Meets the Knowledge Evidence for production processes - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: Enrobing and hand dipping were described as the same process, and three products were matched without a reason. Re-attempt: explain what the enrober does that the hand does not, and give a reason for each product match - NS.

tasks.heading: Task 4 — Historical and cultural origins of chocolates
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — historical and cultural origins of a variety of chocolates.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: (a) 25–40 words per cell · (b) 100 words.
tasks.scenario:
La Meridienne Patisserie, Rundle Street, Adelaide is releasing the Appendix A range as a boxed selection for the winter season. Each box carries a card describing where each chocolate comes from.
Research four chocolate styles from the La Meridienne range and the wider European chocolate tradition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the historical and cultural origins of each chocolate style. Explain how those origins still show in the product made today. Complete the table.

headers: How the origin shows in the product made today

parts.modelAnswer:
Truffle (French truffe) | Developed in France in the late nineteenth century~~Cream and chocolate ganache rolled and dusted in cocoa powder~~Made to resemble the black perigord truffle dug from the ground~~Took its name from that truffle | Irregular rolled shape~~Cocoa or dusted finish rather than a cast, glossy shell~~Short shelf life from the fresh cream centre
Belgian praline (moulded filled shell) | Created in Brussels in 1912 by Jean Neuhaus II~~Cast shell held a soft filling that could not be sold alone~~Belgium built its chocolate industry on the moulded filled shell | Cast shell with a thin even wall~~High gloss from moulding~~Sealed base~~Wide range of soft fillings a shell makes possible
Gianduja | Created in Turin during the Napoleonic blockade~~Early nineteenth century, when cocoa was scarce and expensive~~Piedmont hazelnuts ground in to extend the chocolate | High proportion of hazelnut to cocoa~~Soft melting texture~~Ingot or block shape associated with Piedmont
Torrone or nougat confectionery | Cremona and Montelimar traditions of aerated honey and egg-white confectionery~~Made with nuts~~Made for feast days and Christmas~~Found across Italy, Spain and southern France | Aerated white centre with whole nuts and glace fruit~~Honey sweetness~~Seasonal place in a boxed winter range

satisfactory: (a) all eight cells completed with a genuine historical or cultural origin for each style.
(a) French truffle named for the fungus; Belgian moulded praline from Neuhaus in Brussels.
(a) gianduja from Turin under the Napoleonic blockade.
(a) torrone or nougat from the Italian, Spanish and southern French feast-day tradition.
(a) each origin linked clearly to a feature of the product made today.
(b) explains at least two uses of that knowledge for customers and front-of-house staff.
minimumAcceptable: Three of the four origins substantially correct.
Each carries a plausible link to the product made today.
(b) gives two genuine reasons the knowledge is useful in the shop.
criticalErrors: Origins invented or attributed to the wrong country.
The Belgian praline confused with French praline nut paste.
(a) completed with product descriptions only and no history.
(b) answered under the stated word guide with a single generic reason.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Gave accurate origins for all four styles, including Neuhaus in Brussels in 1912 and the Piedmont hazelnut substitution, and linked each to a feature of the product today. Part (b) covered customer description and allergen honesty - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: Gianduja was attributed to Belgium and the truffle origin was not given. Part (b) said only that it is interesting for customers. Re-attempt: research each style's country and period of origin, and give two specific ways the knowledge helps you describe the range - NS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how knowing these origins helps you describe the range to customers and front-of-house staff.
parts.modelAnswer:
Lets me describe the range accurately at the counter and gives front-of-house the same script.
Explains why the products look and behave differently.
Truffle is rolled and dusted because it imitates a dug truffle.
Belgian praline is glossy and cast because Neuhaus invented the shell to hold a filling.
Helps a customer choose: the story signals texture, sweetness and shelf life, not just heritage.
Supports honest selling: gianduja's hazelnut content matters for a nut allergy.
Lets me say which products are best eaten fresh rather than kept.

tasks.heading: Task 5 — Mise en place and production sequencing
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — mise en place requirements for producing chocolate confectionery.
tasks.scenario:
Friday afternoon service needs 72 individual chocolates: 24 almond croquant (A7), 24 raspberry jelly squares (A9) and 24 caramel bonbons (A3). Use the production data in Appendix B.
The raspberry jelly sets for four hours before cutting. The caramel cools for two hours before piping. Only one tempering machine, one enrobing machine and one set of polished bonbon moulds are available.
You prepare on Thursday and produce on Friday morning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the mise en place you complete on Thursday before production begins. Cover ingredients, equipment, moulds, the work area and the environmental conditions of the room.
parts.modelAnswer:
Read the three standard recipes, scale each to 24 pieces, and check stock and dates.
Weigh and pre-portion the dry ingredients; refrigerate cream and butter until needed.
Clean, dry and switch on the tempering machine to stabilise.
Strip, clean, sanitise, dry and reassemble the enrober with guards fitted.
Check the polished bonbon moulds, polish with cotton wool, bring to room temperature.
Make the jelly (four-hour set) and the caramel (two-hour cool) on Thursday.
Set up separate nut and nut-free benches with colour-coded utensils; label every container.
Confirm transfer sheets, dipping forks, gloves and the probe thermometer are on hand.

satisfactory: (a) covers ingredients, equipment and work area in a logical order for Thursday.
(a) scales the three recipes, checks stock and dates, and pre-weighs.
(a) cleans and prepares the tempering machine, the enrober and the polished moulds.
(a) sets up separate nut and nut-free bench areas.
(b) sequences Thursday and Friday around the four-hour jelly set and the two-hour caramel cool.
(b) respects the single tempering machine, enrober and mould set, and finishes before the 2 pm collection.
minimumAcceptable: (a) covers ingredients, equipment and work area with at least two specific actions each.
(b) makes the jelly and caramel on Thursday for their setting times.
(b) Friday order never puts two products on the tempering machine at once.
criticalErrors: A sequence that ignores the four-hour jelly set or the two-hour caramel cool.
Two products scheduled on the single tempering machine or enrober simultaneously.
The nut product run before nut-free work with no clean-down.
No mention of the moulds in the mise en place.
Production finishing after the 2 pm collection.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Mise en place covered ingredients, equipment and the nut and nut-free bench separation. The sequence placed the jelly and caramel on Thursday for their setting times and staged the Friday tempering machine changeover. Realistic against the 2 pm deadline - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: The plan made the raspberry jelly on Friday morning despite its four-hour set, and ran the croquant before the nut-free work with no clean-down. Re-attempt: build the sequence from the setting times and the single tempering machine, and place the nut product last - NS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sequence the stages of production across Thursday and Friday morning. Justify your order using the setting times and the equipment constraint above.
parts.modelAnswer:
Sequence is driven by setting times and the single tempering machine, enrober and mould set.
Thursday: raspberry jelly first for its four-hour set, then caramel for its two-hour cool.
Thursday: almond croquant slab made last and left to firm overnight.
Friday: temper milk couverture, cast and chill the bonbon shells in the polished moulds.
Pipe the cooled caramel, crust, cap and de-mould.
While the shells set, cut the jelly and the croquant to size.
Change the machine to dark couverture; enrobe the jelly squares and apply transfer sheets.
Hand dip the croquant last, as the nut product, so no nut-free clean-down follows.
Decorate, box and cold store, finished and held before the 2 pm collection.

tasks.heading: Task 6 — Safe operational practices for equipment
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — safe operational practices using essential functions and features of equipment used to produce chocolate confectionery.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: 30–45 words in each writing cell.
tasks.stem: For each item of equipment below, identify its essential functions and features. Explain the safe and hygienic practices you follow when using it. Complete the table.

parts.modelAnswer:
Tempering machine | Heats, holds and cools couverture through a controlled cycle~~Thermostat, stirring auger or wheel, and heated bowl~~Holds large volumes in temper at a set working temperature | Follow the manufacturer instructions for the cycle~~Keep hands, cloths and utensils clear of the auger~~Never add water or wet tools; isolate at the switch before dismantling~~Strip, clean, sanitise and dry the bowl and auger after use
Enrobing machine | Carries centres on a belt under a curtain of tempered couverture~~Pump feeds the curtain and a blower removes excess~~Vibrating table levels the coat~~Cooling tunnel sets it | Guards fitted before starting~~Never reach into the belt, curtain or tunnel while running~~Isolate and lock out before clearing a blockage~~Strip, wash, sanitise and dry the belt and pan after the run
Microwave oven | Heats couverture quickly by agitating water and fat molecules~~Turntable and variable power settings~~Melts small quantities in short bursts | Short bursts at low or medium power, stirring between them~~Bowl heats unevenly and couverture scorches easily~~Use microwave-safe dry bowls and dry cloths to lift them~~Clean and sanitise the cavity after use
Marble slab or bench | Cool, flat, non-porous slab with high thermal mass~~Draws heat out of couverture quickly and evenly~~Stable surface for tabling, cutting and cooling | Sanitise and dry the slab before use, and keep it clear of clutter~~Carry and set down cutting tools away from the working edge~~Never use it as a chopping surface~~Clean and sanitise between products, especially nut and nut-free work
Stove top and saucepan (water jacket) | Saucepan of hot water under a bowl gives indirect, gentle heat~~Variable burner controls the water temperature~~Couverture never in direct contact with the heat | Keep the water below simmering, never boiling into the bowl~~A drop of water will seize the couverture~~Lift with a dry cloth, turning the bowl away from you~~Turn pot handles inwards and switch the burner off before removing the bowl
Digital probe thermometer | Measures couverture and filling temperature to about 0.1 degrees C~~Stainless probe with digital display~~Allows melting and working temperatures to be controlled | Clean and sanitise the probe with an alcohol wipe before and between products~~Calibrate against iced water and record it~~Never leave the probe in the bowl or on the bench~~Store it in its sleeve

satisfactory: All twelve cells completed.
Functions named are the ones that matter in chocolate work, not generic descriptions.
Tempering machine thermostat and auger; enrober curtain, blower, vibrating table and cooling tunnel.
Microwave variable power and turntable; slab thermal mass; water jacket indirect heat; probe accuracy.
Safe operating practice gives a genuine control drawn from manufacturer instructions, not a generic statement.
minimumAcceptable: Ten of twelve cells correct.
Enrober entry names guarding, or isolation before clearing a blockage.
Water jacket entry names the risk of water reaching the couverture.
criticalErrors: Hands in a running enrober or tempering machine.
No isolation or lock-out before dismantling.
A microwave used at full power in a single long burst.
Water or wet tools described as acceptable in the couverture.
Safe practice column filled with be careful or follow instructions and nothing more.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Identified the working functions of all six items and gave specific safety and hygiene practices: isolating the enrober before clearing it, keeping the water jacket below simmering, and sanitising the probe between products. Meets the Knowledge Evidence for safe operational practices - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: The enrober entry did not mention guarding or isolation, and three safe practice cells said only to follow the manufacturer instructions. Re-attempt: name the specific control for each item, including how you make the machine safe before you reach into it - NS.

tasks.heading: Task 7 — Protecting polished chocolate moulds
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — protect polished chocolate moulds from contamination and damage, including ensuring that the polished surface is clean, polished and free of dust or residue; untouched by bare fingers; untouched by objects that may dull, scratch or damage it.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: (a) 30–45 words per cell · (b) 120 words.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each requirement of the polished mould surface, explain why it matters to the finished chocolate. Explain how you achieve and maintain it. Complete the table.

headers: Why it matters to the finished chocolate
How you achieve and maintain it
items: Clean, polished and free of dust or residue
Untouched by objects that may dull, scratch or damage it

parts.modelAnswer:
Clean, polished and free of dust or residue | Dust, residue or fat film stops full contact with the mould~~Finished chocolate comes out dull, patchy or marked~~Loses the mirror gloss the moulded face needs | Polish each cavity with cotton wool or a lint-free cloth before every run~~Check under a good light~~Wash only when necessary in warm water, leaving no detergent film~~Dry fully before polishing
Untouched by bare fingers | Skin leaves a fatty fingerprint that shows as a dull mark~~Bare hands are also a food safety risk~~Mould is in direct contact with ready-to-eat food | Wear food-safe gloves~~Handle moulds by the edges and the frame only~~Change gloves after handling anything else~~Never rest fingers in a cavity when carrying a mould
Untouched by objects that may dull, scratch or damage it | A scratch or a dulled patch is permanent~~Reproduced on every chocolate cast in that cavity~~Loses gloss and can stop the piece releasing cleanly | Keep metal scrapers, knives, abrasive pads and scourers off the cavities~~Scrape the mould face only with a plastic or nylon scraper~~Stack moulds face to back with a liner between them

satisfactory: (a) all six cells completed.
(a) each requirement justified by loss of gloss, marks reproduced on every cast, or failure to release.
(a) each requirement paired with a practical method of achieving and maintaining it.
(b) cleaning with a plastic scraper, washing only when needed, drying fully.
(b) polishing cavity by cavity.
(b) storing interleaved in a dry area at steady temperature, away from heat and metal tools.
minimumAcceptable: Five of six cells in (a) correct.
(a) a correct reason given for the bare-fingers requirement.
(b) covers polishing, dry storage and protection from scratching.
criticalErrors: Moulds washed with detergent and scoured, or dried with abrasive cloth.
Metal scrapers or knives described as acceptable on the cavity face.
Bare-hand handling accepted.
A scratch described as removable by polishing.
No reference to gloss or release in the reasons.
benchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Explained why each requirement matters in terms of gloss, permanent marking and release, and described handling by the edges with food-safe gloves. Storage answer covered plastic scrapers, full drying, cavity polishing and interleaved dry storage - S.
benchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: The answer said scratches can be polished out and described scouring the moulds. Re-attempt: explain that a scratch is permanent and is reproduced on every chocolate cast in that cavity, and state what may and may not touch the polished face - NS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At La Meridienne Patisserie, Rundle Street, Adelaide, explain how you handle and store the polished bonbon moulds between production runs. Show how this prevents contamination and damage.
parts.modelAnswer:
Scrape clean with a plastic scraper between runs and check under a good light.
Wash only if there is a residue that will not lift.
Use warm water without detergent, or the detergent the manufacturer specifies.

tasks.heading: Task 8 — Seed crystals and tempering methods
tasks.mapsTo: Knowledge Evidence — tempering methods for couverture: controlling the formation of seed crystals; tabling method; use of heated water jackets; use of microwave; vaccination or addition method.
tasks.wordGuide: Word guide: (a) 120 words · (b) 45–60 words per cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what seed crystals are in couverture. Explain how controlling their formation produces correctly tempered chocolate.
parts.modelAnswer:
Cocoa butter can set in several different crystal forms.
Only the beta or form V crystal gives gloss, a clean snap and reliable release.
Seed crystals are small stable beta crystals already present in the couverture.
They act as a template the rest of the cocoa butter builds on as it solidifies.
Melt to close to 40 degrees C, which destroys all crystal forms.
Cool so crystals form again, then bring back to the working temperature.
Unstable forms melt out and only the stable beta seed remains.
Too little seed sets soft, dull and streaky; too much thickens and is hard to work.

satisfactory: (a) cocoa butter sets in several crystal forms; only the stable beta form gives gloss, snap and release.
(a) seed crystals are stable beta crystals acting as a template.
(a) melt to close to 40 degrees C to destroy all crystal forms.
(a) cool to form crystals, then hold at the working temperature so unstable forms melt out.
(a) consequences of too little and too much seed are given.
(b) all eight cells completed, with a workable method for each of the four methods.
(b) a genuine advantage and a genuine limitation for each method.
minimumAcceptable: (a) names the stable beta or form V crystal.
(a) explains seeding as a template.
(a) gives the melt and working stages.
(b) six of eight cells correct.
(b) vaccination method described as seed reserved from the batch.
criticalErrors: Tempering described only as heating and cooling, with no reference to crystal form.
Seed described as an additive bought separately rather than couverture already in temper.
Vaccination method described as adding seed on top of the total weight.
A limitation given that is not a limitation, such as needs chocolate.

parts.modelAnswer:

Use of heated water jackets | Set a bowl over a saucepan of hot, not boiling, water~~Melt the couverture to close to 40 degrees C~~Remove the bowl and dry its base~~Cool with stirring, over cool water if needed, to working temperature | Advantage: gentle, even heat using equipment every kitchen has~~Limitation: steam or a drop of water will seize the couverture~~Limitation: holding temperature steady on a long run needs constant attention
Use of microwave | Heat about three quarters in a microwave-safe bowl~~Use 20 second bursts, stirring after each~~Stop when nearly melted and close to 40 degrees C~~Stir in the reserved quarter until melted and at working temperature | Advantage: fast and clean for small batches, no water near the bowl~~Limitation: heats unevenly and scorches white and milk couverture~~Limitation: unsuitable for production run volumes

parts.text: Explain the requirements for storing and displaying these products under the Food Act 2001 (SA) and Standards 3.2.2 and 3.2.2A of the Food Standards Code. State the role of the local council environmental health officer.
parts.modelAnswer:
The patisserie is a food business under the Food Act 2001 (SA).
It must comply with the Food Standards Code, in particular Standards 3.2.2 and 3.2.2A.
It sells unpackaged, ready-to-eat, potentially hazardous food containing dairy directly to consumers.
Passionfruit ganache chocolates must be kept at 5 degrees C or below for the whole 48 hours.
Or under another regime the business can demonstrate is safe; temperature monitored and recorded.
Unpackaged display must be protected from contamination: covers or screens, tongs not hands, no unprotected self-service.
Standard 3.2.2A requires a food safety supervisor and evidence of temperature control and cleaning and sanitising.
Regulator is SA Health; council environmental health officers inspect and can require corrective action or prohibit sale.

extractionNotes: Dash character: every task heading in the learner document uses an em dash (U+2014), e.g. "Task 7 — Protecting polished chocolate moulds".
